newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus seen rising after 2-year lull.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus seen rising after 2-year lull.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus is expected to rise in February for the first time in over two years on the back of the yen's weakening, and economists say it may lead to renewed trade friction in the longer term.
They forecast a merchandise trade surplus of 698.4 billion yen ($5.72 billion) on average for February, up from a 648.0 billion yen ($5.31 billion) surplus in February 1996.
If the data, to be announced on Monday, were to show a rise in the surplus, it would be the first year-on-year increase since November 1994.
A rise in the surplus would mainly be due to the weakening of the yen, which has accelerated Japan's exports while putting the brakes on imports, economists said.
"It's the effect of the weak yen. The rise in exports, led by cars, is spreading to export industries as a whole," said Yoshito Sakakibara, vice president at Salomon Brothers Asia.

In the first 20 days of February, Japan's trade surplus rose 53.3 percent from the same period a year earlier, and the data showed that exports had risen 15.2 percent while imports had gained 12.8 percent.
The figures mask the real size of the trend since the lower yen pushes down the overall value of exports while increasing the domestic price of imports.
DKB Research Institute expects Japanese exports in February to show a year-on-year increase of 3.2 percent in quantitative terms, against a 2.5 percent drop for imports.
Economists said a rise in Japan's surplus posed a potential source of trade friction with countries such as the United States.
Earlier this month, U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers urged Tokyo to make sure its recovery was led by domestic growth and that its trade surplus did not surge.
"But in fact, it's a recovery brought on by external demand," said Salomon's Sakakibara.
Japan's trade surplus fell 91.7 percent in January from a year earlier, but its trade surplus with the United States rose a sharp 81.6 percent.
Japan's vehicle exports to the United States shot up 75.3 percent in January, reflecting the yen's fall against the dollar.
Although U.S. authorities have so far given no hint of using the currency rate as a tool to control trade imbalances, economists said a rise in Japan's surplus would put upward pressure on the yen.

"The U.S. has said it does not intend to use the forex rate (to manipulate the trade balance), but present moves (of a rise in Japan's surplus) are precisely due to the forex rate. There's a gap between the two," said Salomon's Sakakibara.
